items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why salt weathering is important in hot deserts. (b) A student writes: “Freeze-thaw is most effective in places with permanently frozen ground.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Saline groundwater is drawn to the surface by capillary action; evaporation causes salt crystals to grow in pores, exerting pressure; heating also expands salts. (b) Not correct. It needs repeated cycles of freezing and thawing; permanently frozen ground has few cycles.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 4.1 shows a midday energy budget (W/m²) for a surface of grassland on a clear day: incoming solar radiation 820; reflected solar radiation 205; net long-wave radiation loss 80; latent heat transfer (evaporation) 168; surface absorption 70; sensible heat transfer to the air: not shown. Suggest why the albedo of this surface could change during the year.
items.answer: Snow cover, leaf fall, crop growth or harvest, wetness, sun angle (especially for water).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Women often have less secure access to land than men in rural LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the problems of providing services in rural areas of LICs.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Customary inheritance and legal systems frequently favour men. (b) Dispersed population and long distances; poor roads; low incomes; difficulty attracting teachers and doctors; high costs per person.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Using one named example of an informal settlement, evaluate the attempts to improve the settlement.
items.answer: Kibera, Nairobi: Kenya Slum Upgrading Programme (KENSUP) built blocks of flats at Soweto East; railway relocation; NGO water kiosks and bio-centres; limited impact because rents rose and many original residents did not benefit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Schemes, dates, success and limitations. [5]

items.stem: Engineers estimated the shear strength and shear stress (kPa) on three slopes beside roads in Hong Kong. Slope A: shear strength 59, shear stress 146. Slope B: shear strength 41, shear stress 48. Slope C: shear strength 99, shear stress 130. (a) Calculate the factor of safety (shear strength ÷ shear stress) for each slope. (b) Identify which slopes are likely to fail. (c) Suggest two ways engineers could increase the factor of safety of an unstable slope.
items.answer: (a) Slope A 0.4; Slope B 0.85; Slope C 0.76 (b) Slope A, Slope B, Slope C (factor of safety below 1) (c) Drainage to lower pore water pressure; regrading to a lower angle; retaining walls or rock bolts; soil nailing; vegetation; removing load from the top.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark two correct; 2 marks all [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 7.2 shows the age of basalt samples at different distances from the East Pacific Rise: 250 km: 5 million years, 550 km: 11 million years, 700 km: 14 million years, 800 km: 16 million years. (a) Calculate the mean rate of spreading (cm per year) on this side of the ridge, using the furthest sample. (b) Describe the relationship between distance from the ridge and age of the rocks. (c) Explain how this evidence supports sea-floor spreading. (d) Explain why no oceanic crust older than about 200 million years exists.
items.answer: (a) 5 cm per year (b) Age increases with distance from the ridge in a near-linear way. (c) New crust forms at the ridge and is carried away as the plates diverge, so the youngest rocks are at the ridge and older ones further away, symmetrically on each side. (d) Older, colder, denser crust is subducted and destroyed at trenches.

items.stem: Fig. 18.1 is based on bid-rent theory. The rent (US$ per m² per year) each land use is willing to pay falls with distance d (km) from the CBD: retail: 1107 − 311d; offices and industry: 587 − 104d; housing: 283 − 33d. (a) Calculate the distance at which offices and industry outbid retail. (b) Calculate the distance at which housing outbids offices and industry. (c) Calculate the distance beyond which no urban land use will pay rent. (d) Explain why retail can pay the highest rents near the CBD.
items.answer: (a) 2.51 km (b) 4.28 km (c) 8.58 km (d) The centre is the most accessible point, so shops attract the most customers (high threshold and range) and make high profits; they need little space.

items.stem: Leila argues that human activity has a greater effect than physical factors on the transfers of water within a drainage basin. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to rock type and rainfall intensity.
items.answer: For: Urbanisation replaces permeable soil with concrete, cutting infiltration; deforestation removes interception; field drains and channelisation speed throughflow and channel flow. Against: Rock permeability, soil type, slope and vegetation set the basic pattern of transfers; climate (rainfall intensity, frozen ground) controls overland flow in most basins. Conclusion: Physical factors set the baseline in all basins, but in heavily modified (urban or deforested) basins human activity dominates transfers.

Rock permeability, soil type, slope and vegetation set the basic pattern of transfers; climate (rainfall intensity, frozen ground) controls overland flow in most basins. Judgement: Physical factors set the baseline in all basins, but in heavily modified (urban or deforested) basins human activity dominates transfers.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the costs of international migration are greater than the benefits for source countries? In your answer you may refer to demographic change and remittances.
items.answer: For: Brain drain of doctors and nurses (Zimbabwe, Philippines); ageing; family breakdown; labour shortages; dependency on remittances. Against: Remittances exceed aid and reduce poverty; reduced unemployment; return of skilled migrants; diaspora investment and trade links (India’s IT sector). Conclusion: For most source countries the economic benefits outweigh the costs, but the balance depends on how many skilled workers leave and how remittances are used.

items.stem: Table 6.2 shows mean annual precipitation (mm) along a transect across the Western Ghats, India, in the direction of the prevailing wind: windward coast (0 m) 1 294, windward slope (800 m) 2 288, summit (1500 m) 3 210, leeward slope (800 m) 753, leeward lowland (100 m) 323. (a) Explain the increase in precipitation up the windward slope. (b) Explain why the leeward side is much drier.
items.answer: (a) Moist air is forced to rise (orographic uplift), cools adiabatically to dew point, condenses into cloud and rain; uplift may trigger instability. (b) Air has lost much moisture on the windward side; descending air warms adiabatically at the DALR, so relative humidity falls and clouds evaporate (rain shadow).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per stage [3] (b) 1 mark moisture lost; 1 mark descending warming [2]

items.stem: The population of Lagos grew from 7 million in 1990 to 11.7 million in 2010. Natural increase within the city accounted for 41% of the growth; the rest came from net in-migration. (a) Calculate the mean annual growth rate (compound). (b) Explain two consequences of this growth for the city.
items.answer: (a) 2.6% per year (b) Informal settlements expand; shortages of water, sanitation and power; traffic congestion; informal sector employment; pressure on schools and health care.
items.markingKey: (a) (11.7 ÷ 7)^(1/20) − 1 [3] (b) 1 mark each with development [4]

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): South Korea: 1955-1985; Sweden: 1810-1930; Brazil: 1960-2005; Japan: 1920-1960. (a) Calculate the mean length of the transition for these countries. (b) Describe the relationship between the start date and the length of the transition. (c) Explain why later transitions were faster.
items.answer: (a) 58.8 years (b) Countries that began later generally completed it faster. (c) Access to modern contraception and medicine; family-planning programmes (Bangladesh, Iran); rapid urbanisation and female education; mass media spreading new norms.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark per reason [3]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Hail is most common in summer thunderstorms.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Strong convection is needed to produce the updraughts that keep hailstones in the cloud.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [5]

items.stem: Table 15.1 shows approximate remittance inflows and GDP (US$ billion, 2023): Pakistan: remittances 27, GDP 338; Nepal: remittances 11, GDP 41; Guatemala: remittances 20, GDP 104; India: remittances 120, GDP 3 550. Explain why a country can receive large remittances but not be very dependent on them.
items.answer: A large economy (high GDP) means even large remittances are a small share of national income, e.g. India or Mexico.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Hard engineering can create a false sense of security.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Dams have no effect on rivers downstream.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. People build behind levees; when they are overtopped, as in New Orleans in 2005, damage is greater. (b) Not correct. They trap sediment, alter regimes and cause downstream channel erosion and delta retreat.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A surveyor measured an unstable cut slope above a road in Hanoi’s hinterland. It rises 7.6 m over a horizontal distance of 18 m. (a) Calculate the slope angle in degrees. (b) Explain why regrading increases slope stability.
items.answer: (a) 22.9° (b) A lower angle reduces the downslope component of gravity (shear stress), so the factor of safety increases.

items.stem: Table 7.2 shows the age of basalt samples at different distances from the Carlsberg Ridge (Indian Ocean): 100 km: 2.9 million years, 250 km: 7.1 million years, 300 km: 8.6 million years, 750 km: 21.4 million years. (a) Calculate the mean rate of spreading (cm per year) on this side of the ridge, using the furthest sample. (b) Calculate the full rate at which the two plates are separating, assuming symmetrical spreading. (c) Explain how this evidence supports sea-floor spreading.
items.answer: (a) 3.5 cm per year (b) 7 cm per year (c) New crust forms at the ridge and is carried away as the plates diverge, so the youngest rocks are at the ridge and older ones further away, symmetrically on each side.

items.stem: Country Q had a population of 60 million, a crude birth rate of 23 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 13 per 1000. In the same year 342 000 people immigrated and 597 000 emigrated. (a) Calculate the natural increase (number of people). (b) Calculate the total population change and state which component contributed more. (c) Suggest one demographic effect of this migration on the country.
items.answer: (a) 600 000 (b) +345 000; natural change contributed more. (c) Loses young adults, so the population ages and future births fall.
items.markingKey: (a) (23 − 13) per 1000 × 60 million [2] (b) natural change + net migration [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows the population structure (%) of Country J, with a projection for 2040: 2000: 0-14 17%, 15-64 68%, 65+ 15%. 2020: 0-14 18%, 15-64 62%, 65+ 20%. 2040: 0-14 12%, 15-64 54%, 65+ 34%. (a) Calculate the old-age dependency ratio for each year. (b) Calculate the number of people of working age per person aged 65+ in 2040. (c) Explain two consequences of the projected change.
items.answer: (a) 2000 22.1; 2020 32.3; 2040 63 (b) 1.59 (c) Higher pension and health-care costs; fewer taxpayers per pensioner; labour shortages; greater demand for care workers; possible rise in retirement age.
items.markingKey: (a) 65+ ÷ 15-64 × 100 [2] (b) 54 ÷ 34 [1] (c) 1 mark each with development [4]

items.stem: “Overpopulation is caused more by unequal distribution of resources than by population growth.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to consumption, technology and food distribution.
items.answer: For: Global food production is enough for all; hunger results from poverty, conflict, waste and unequal access; HICs consume far more per person. Against: Rapid growth in the Sahel and parts of South Asia does increase pressure on land, water and fuelwood; resource limits are real in fragile environments. Conclusion: Both matter, but inequality of access and consumption explains more of the imbalance than population numbers alone.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the problems of megacities outweigh their benefits.
items.answer: For: Congestion, pollution (Delhi), informal housing (Mumbai’s Dharavi), water shortages, flooding (Jakarta), inequality. Against: Megacities generate a large share of national GDP, innovation and jobs; economies of scale make services cheaper per person; they offer opportunities to migrants; well-managed examples (Tokyo). Conclusion: Problems are severe in fast-growing LIC megacities, but benefits are large; the balance depends on governance and investment.

items.stem: Station X (Lagos, Nigeria) has a mean annual temperature of 27 °C and rainfall of 1 500 mm. Station Y (Reykjavík, Iceland) has 5 °C and 850 mm. (a) Using the Peltier diagram, identify the likely weathering regime at each station. (b) Explain the difference between the two stations. (c) Suggest one limitation of the Peltier diagram.
items.answer: (a) X: strong chemical weathering; Y: frost action (freeze-thaw) dominant (b) Explanation in terms of temperature (reaction rates, freeze-thaw around 0 °C) and water availability. (c) Uses annual means, hiding seasonal and diurnal variations; ignores rock type, vegetation and microclimate.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark temperature; 1 mark moisture [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: A survey of 40 return migrants in a village in Kerala, India recorded their main reason for returning: family obligations 3, retirement 9, savings target reached 2, could not find work 20, better opportunities at home 6. (a) Calculate the percentage of returnees who gave “could not find work”. (b) Calculate the angle needed for “could not find work” on a pie chart. (c) Suggest how the reasons could be grouped into positive and negative reasons for return. (d) Explain how returnees may affect the economy of the area.
items.answer: (a) 50% (b) 180° (c) Positive: savings target, retirement, better opportunities at home; negative: could not find work; family obligations can be either. (d) Investing savings in houses, land and businesses; bringing skills; creating jobs; but pressure on local jobs if many return at once.

items.stem: In one year Country P, with a mid-year population of 4.2 million, recorded 37 800 live births, 54 600 deaths and 1 701 deaths of infants under one year old. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase as a percentage. (b) Calculate the infant mortality rate. (c) Suggest whether this country is an LIC or an HIC, using the data.
items.answer: (a) −0.4% (b) 45 per 1000 live births (c) Probably a middle-income country: indicators are intermediate or mixed.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the impacts of migration change over time. (b) A student writes: “Receiving countries gain nothing from migration.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Initial pressures ease as migrants integrate; migrants age and may return; second generations change; economic cycles and policies alter flows. (b) Not correct. Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes and contribute to economic growth.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 16.2 shows the percentage of farmland held by different groups of landholders in a district in Bihar, India: largest 10% of holdings 62%, next 20% 25%, middle 30% 10%, smallest 40% 3%. Describe the distribution of land.
items.answer: Very unequal: the largest 10% of holdings have 62% of the land, while the smallest 40% have only 3%.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Classify mass movements by speed and water content. (b) Explain why rotational slides are common on clay slopes.
items.answer: (a) Heaves (creep) slow and moderately wet; flows (mudflows, earthflows) fast and wet; slides (rotational, translational) fast, moderately dry along a slip plane; falls very fast and dry. (b) Clay becomes saturated and loses strength; it is weak and impermeable, so water builds up; slopes over-steepened by river or wave erosion fail along a curved plane.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per type [4] (b) [3]

items.stem: Using one named example of a river landform or delta, describe the opportunities and challenges the landform presents for people.
items.answer: the Nile delta, Egypt: Holds about 40% of Egypt’s population and most farmland; since the Aswan High Dam (1970) traps sediment, the coast retreats by up to 100 m a year in places such as Rosetta; salinisation and subsidence.

items.stem: Elena argues that cloud cover is the most important factor influencing local energy budgets. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Clouds reflect incoming solar radiation by day and give counter-radiation at night, so they reduce the diurnal range (e.g. humid tropics v deserts). Against: Surface albedo, moisture availability (latent heat), wind speed (sensible heat), season and latitude (sun angle), and urban surfaces also control budgets. Conclusion: Cloud cover is crucial for the diurnal range, but surface characteristics and sun angle decide how much energy is available in the first place.

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): South Korea: 1955-1985; England and Wales: 1800-1940; Iran: 1985-2005; Japan: 1920-1960. (a) Calculate the length of the fertility transition in each country. (b) Describe the relationship between the start date and the length of the transition. (c) Suggest what this means for the usefulness of the DTM.
items.answer: (a) South Korea 30 years; England and Wales 140 years; Iran 20 years; Japan 40 years (b) Countries that began later generally completed it faster. (c) The sequence holds but the timescale varies, so the DTM cannot predict timing and must be adapted for LICs.

items.stem: A survey of 50 households in an informal settlement in Manila found the number of households with: piped water inside the home: 25; a private toilet: 11; electricity: 31; a member working in the informal sector: 19; a member who migrated from a rural area: 14. (a) Suggest a suitable method of presenting these results. (b) Suggest how the households could be sampled to make the results representative. (c) Explain how the lack of services could affect residents’ health and livelihoods.
items.answer: (a) A bar chart (percentages for each service), as the categories are not parts of one whole, so a pie chart is unsuitable. (b) Systematic sampling of every nth dwelling along transects, or stratified sampling by zone of the settlement; random starting point; avoid only main paths. (c) Lack of clean water and sanitation spreads diarrhoeal disease and cholera; time spent collecting water; illness reduces earnings; women and girls most affected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark justification [2] (b) [2] (c) [3]

items.stem: A model based on Malthus assumes population (millions) doubles every 30 years from 2 million, while food supply (enough for millions of people) rises by 1 million every 30 years from 2 million. Values: year 0: population 2, food 2; year 30: population 4, food 3; year 60: population 8, food 4; year 90: population 16, food 5; year 120: population 32, food 6. (a) Identify the year in which population first exceeds food supply. (b) Calculate the shortfall in food supply in year 180. (c) Suggest one real-world example that supports each theorist.
items.answer: (a) year 30 (b) 120 million people (c) Malthus: famines in the Sahel or Ethiopia (1984). Boserup: Green Revolution in India; terracing in Machakos, Kenya (“more people, less erosion”).

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “The gravity model predicts more migration between large, nearby cities.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why migration is often selective by age.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Flows are proportional to population size and decrease with distance. (b) Young adults have fewest ties, most to gain from new jobs and education, and can adapt; older people have property and family commitments.

items.stem: Classify each ocean current as warm or cold: Canary Current, Agulhas Current, Gulf Stream, California Current, Kuroshio Current, Benguela Current. Explain the effect of one cold current on the climate of the adjacent coast.
items.answer: Canary Current cold; Agulhas Current warm; Gulf Stream warm; California Current cold; Kuroshio Current warm; Benguela Current cold. Cold currents cool the air above, creating stable conditions, little rain and advection fog (e.g. Benguela and the Namib desert).

items.stem: “Atmospheric stability is the most important factor in determining the type of precipitation an area receives.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to moisture and temperature.
items.answer: For: Unstable air produces convective showers, thunderstorms and hail; stable air gives drizzle, fog and dry weather. Against: Temperature (rain, snow or hail), moisture supply, uplift mechanisms (relief, fronts, convergence), condensation nuclei and cloud processes also matter. Conclusion: Stability controls whether air rises far enough to give heavy precipitation, but moisture and temperature control the amount and form.

items.stem: “Chemical weathering is the most important type of weathering in all environments.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to periglacial areas and rock type.
items.answer: For: Chemical weathering dominates in the humid tropics (weathering profiles over 60 m deep); carbonation shapes limestone landscapes worldwide; hydrolysis produces clays. Against: In cold and arid environments physical weathering (freeze-thaw, salt crystal growth) dominates because water or warmth is limited; biological weathering matters in vegetated areas. Conclusion: Chemical weathering is the most widespread and effective globally, but not in all environments.

items.stem: A student draws a flow diagram of the drainage basin system for a small upland catchment in the Pennines, UK, with peat moorland on impermeable gritstone. (a) Distinguish between infiltration and percolation. (b) Explain how saturated peat on impermeable rock would affect the transfers shown. (c) Suggest how one human activity could increase the output of water from this basin.
items.answer: (a) Infiltration is water entering the soil surface; percolation is water moving down from the soil into the rock below. (b) Infiltration and percolation are low; most water moves as saturated overland flow or throughflow in the peat; little groundwater and baseflow, so rapid flood peaks. (c) Drainage ditches (gripping) on the moor or clearing vegetation speed flows and increase discharge; reservoirs may increase evaporation.

items.stem: Freya argues that the tri-cellular model fully explains global patterns of pressure and winds. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to continentality and jet streams.
items.answer: For: It explains the equatorial low, subtropical highs, mid-latitude westerlies, sub-polar lows and polar highs, and the trade winds. Against: Real patterns are disrupted by continents and oceans (seasonal Asian high and low), relief, ocean currents, jet streams and Rossby waves, monsoons and the seasonal shift of belts with the overhead sun. Conclusion: The model explains the broad zonal pattern well but not regional and seasonal variations.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that Boserup’s ideas are more relevant than those of Malthus in the 21st century. In your answer you may refer to technology and climate change.
items.answer: For: Green Revolution, GM crops, precision farming and trade have raised food output faster than population; global famine has not occurred. Against: Neo-Malthusian concerns: climate change, water stress, soil degradation, biodiversity loss; local famines (Somalia 2011) and food insecurity persist; innovation may not keep pace in fragile areas. Conclusion: Boserup better describes global trends so far, but Malthusian limits remain relevant locally and environmentally.

items.stem: Table 7.2 shows the age of basalt samples at different distances from the East Pacific Rise: 50 km: 1 million years, 100 km: 2 million years, 350 km: 7 million years, 850 km: 17 million years. items.answer: (a) 5 cm per year (b) Age increases with distance from the ridge in a near-linear way. items.stem: At 18:00 on a clear, calm autumn evening the air temperature at a weather station was 9 °C and the dew point was 6 °C. The temperature then fell steadily by 0.5 °C per hour.
